comments.author: @AldrickTanith
comments.text:
Alright, let’s be real—this Blueprint isn’t about helping everyone. It’s about OpenAI making sure they stay on top. They’re pushing for nationwide regulations, but who do you think that really helps? The little guy trying to innovate? Nope. It’s the big corporations like OpenAI that can afford to play by those rules while smaller developers get buried under red tape. This isn’t about fairness—it’s about locking in power.

And then there’s the whole ‘national security’ angle. OpenAI is clearly using tech nationalism as a ploy to grab more influence and secure government funding. Sure, nation-states might see AI as a national security issue, but the constant ‘China is coming!’ narrative feels like a convenient excuse to funnel money into big tech. Let’s not forget—if OpenAI can’t get the funding they want from the U.S., they’ll go elsewhere. They’re not loyal to the United States or any other country—they’re loyal to profit. That’s how corporations work; the bottom line always comes first. What AI really needs isn’t this kind of tech nationalism. It needs global collaboration to ensure AI aligns with human goals—not just the agendas of nation-states or profit-driven corporations.

As things stand, most of the so-called ‘economic benefits’ aren’t going to trickle down to regular people. They’re going to line the pockets of corporations and investors. OpenAI is wrapping this in fancy language like ‘innovation’ and ‘progress,’ but let’s call it what it really is—a power grab.

If OpenAI truly cared about democratizing AI, they’d be advocating for transparency, accountability, open-source solutions (like they originally claimed to stand for), and global collaboration. Instead, they’re writing a playbook to monopolize the industry.

So much to unpack. 
British national, living in Denmark, working for company based in US and China. In other words, prioritising quality of life, while acknowledging economic reality.

comments.author: @SmarttStuff
comments.text:
This may be a long post - Yes Wes  'interesting' you may say,..and you run a good channel, and provide varied, and also controversial perspectives in this space. I am also appreciative of the amazing creative work of all the AI companies and labs that are part of this wave. AI even in it's current form now, is delivering substantial benefits to society, and should continue.

However this paper is a terrible idea. Any thinking human will quickly pick up on the bias. Frankly most democratically-minded people would roll their eyes, because we have seen this all before. People everywhere are tired of being dictated to by any authority, be that an inept government, an ambitious corporation, a dictator, or a military power.

In times gone by Church and State united to oppress the masses. Then it was noticed that such concentration of power would corrupt totally, so the alliance was disbanded, not without blood though. Now we see the alliance of powerful Business with State, which is just another corrupt version of the same. This paper just throws into focus many things that are wrong with our world. AI is a lens that is challenging us to look at ourselves. AI is not the problem - we are.

So are all technologies created for entrenching power ?? This is a sad and dismal view, lacking in any humanity, or good sense. I am a strong advocate of the benefits of technology for humankind, not for the adding of more suffering for humankind. These power moves are indeed scary and do not bode well for the future. AI companies cannot talk about competing fiercely, and at the same time refer to democratisation, they should know that is an oxymoron.

The One-Winner idea is flawed. This way there will be a dominant winner and everyone else will lose (btw are already losing). The super-competitive approach seems like the right thing to do, but it will result in exactly the opposite outcome. It becomes very clear, when one is on the outside of a problem, to see the flaws and even some potentials for doing it differently. When you live in any country, it is natural to adopt that perspective, and reason that is the only viewpoint. A fear-based motivation is not the right starting-point for development, it is by nature anti-life. A truly positive motivation focuses on the ways to benefit society. One cannot, in fairness expect that kind of vision from a profit-seeking enterprise, or a state-security apparatus, they are self-centred and myopic about their fundamental purposes. We expected democratic governance to be able to reconcile these issues and deliver a fair solution for people at large. The biggest thing to learn, is that any concentration of power will corrupt the system that has that power. The drug that humans are addicted to is Power, and it is corrosive. This quickly becomes a discussion around deeper things like true values, destiny of humankind, what purpose is, what wisdom is, what is the meaning of it all? 

Take a little step back and put yourself in the shoes of a Ukranian. How do you think you would feel about your future? do you see promise, can you see children, and happy life ahead? No you would not. Now take another step, this time forward ... The AI/ASI race has been won, by anyone. Looking forward do you see a free and open future, one brimming with possibility, a future where human suffering is substantially reduced, where people have newfound purpose, where hope abides, and humanity thrives? Ask yourself 'what do we need to do to get there?" (your gut will tell you). It will probably not be a centralised solution, or a corporate plan, but perhaps a new concept where individual sovereignty is core. We should explore how to do that, and perhaps it is up to the individual to seek that out. It has to be bottom-up, otherwise we have the perpetual fail as in every century before.

When it comes to really big challenges(problems), We as a species don't actually think very broadly at all, more a localised myopia is what we do. Often it is a one-shot of our neural nets, just predicting the next obvious idea. We do short term calculations, and kick the can down the road mostly. To really think deeply, responsibly, wisely and with vision and positivity is really very, very difficult to do. I really hope there are some very bright human minds, coupled to bright AI minds that tackle these kinds of challenges. If we left it to one country, one corporation, one lab, one viewpoint, one committee, one CEO, one Poliitical view - it will be a disaster.

We can change willingly, or be forced by events, but change is the only inevitable thing. We have it in ourselves to be creative and see things differently. We desperately need to address the ways we think about our future, and our place in it. Emphasis on WE.

I am from South Africa.

comments.author: @abnejne4737
comments.text:
I'm old enough to have lived without the internet and mobile phones, and I've always been very positive about technology and the changes it brings. I've also been interested in AI for many years, but I never thought it would become this advanced in my lifetime—at least not until a few years ago. Now, for the first time in my life, technology is making me nervous about the future. There are so many ways it can go wrong and be misused. And looking back at human history, it's hard not to think it will be used to control and enslave people.

When states and the wealthy individuals who control mega-corporations no longer need ordinary people, will they really share the wealth, or will they view us as a problem to be dealt with? If an AI dictatorship is ever installed, how would anyone fight it? With total surveillance of everything, everywhere, all the time, you wouldn't even need humans to enforce it. Drones and robots are advancing rapidly, and a very small group of people could control an entire country—or perhaps even the world—without much opposition.

It seems that humanity is on the brink of creating something that could serve as the foundation for a dystopian world far beyond what Orwell could have imagined in 1984. It's not so much a question of whether the technology can be used for the greater good. Rather, it's a question of whether we can trust the people who control it.
